overview: This file concerns complaints about Japanese postal service delays, censorship, and confiscation of foreign periodicals, especially those raised by the Reverend Harold J. Schenck of Yokohama. Its principal sequence consists of cross-reference sheets, a May 1936 despatch from American Consul Richard F. Boyce, and an enclosed Japanese postal official’s explanation of censorship policy, including its connection to protection of the national polity and prevention of lèse-majesté. A separate 1933 State Department memorandum records Stanley K. Hornbeck’s preparation of draft correspondence in response to an earlier, unspecified matter involving Mr. Stern and senators from Indiana.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Boyce Despatch No. 202 on mail delays and confiscated magazines
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to another file containing Despatch No. 202 concerning Japanese postal delays and Harold J. Schenck’s complaint about confiscated foreign magazines.
subfiles.summary: This filing note points to document 125.0666/167 for Boyce’s Despatch No. 202 from Yokohama. It describes the referenced despatch as reporting delays in mail from the United States and enclosing Schenck’s complaint about the confiscation of foreign magazines.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Yokohama despatch on Japanese censorship of foreign mail
subfiles.about: The sheet refers readers to a despatch explaining Japanese censorship of foreign mail in response to Harold Schenck.
subfiles.summary: The filing note directs readers to another decimal-file location for Despatch No. 10 from Yokohama. Its date is normalized as May 7, 1936, matching the despatch on the following page; the OCR renders the date as “1-7, 1936” and Boyce’s surname as “Borge.”

subfiles.title: Boyce despatch enclosing a Japanese explanation of postal censorship
subfiles.about: Boyce forwards a Japanese official’s reply to Harold J. Schenck concerning the delivery, censorship, and confiscation of correspondence and printed matter arriving from abroad.
subfiles.summary: Boyce refers to his earlier despatches about Japanese handling and censorship of foreign correspondence and printed matter. He encloses a May 2 reply to Schenck that illustrates the Japanese authorities’ attitude toward the issue and notes that it answered Schenck’s letter of April 25.

subfiles.title: Japanese postal official’s reply to Harold J. Schenck
subfiles.to: Harold J. Schenck, Union Church, Yokohama
subfiles.about: A Japanese postal official explains and defends the principles governing censorship and confiscation of domestic and foreign periodicals.
subfiles.summary: The official declines to issue the broad public policy statement Schenck requested and refers his letter to the Director General of Posts in Tokyo. He asserts that periodicals are judged without regard to country, language, nationality, or the recipient’s identity and that seizure depends upon content. The letter links stringent censorship to protection of Japan’s national polity and the prevention of lèse-majesté, while asking foreign residents to show the same patience as Japanese citizens. It treats removal of individual objectionable pages as administratively burdensome but potentially acceptable if it does not involve excessive labor or expense, and closes by praising Schenck’s work for Japanese-American friendship.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum to Hackworth urging prompt action
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hornbeck submits a memorandum and two tentative draft letters for rapid review because Mr. Stern requested prompt action and the matter could affect relations with Indiana senators.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains that he prepared two draft letters provisionally and invites Hackworth to replace them if he favors a different response. He emphasizes Mr. Stern’s request for prompt action and suggests that expedition would assist the Department in dealing with senators from Indiana. The referenced memorandum and draft letters are not present in this file segment.

interest: The most valuable material is the enclosed Japanese explanation of how postal censorship was justified and administered in the mid-1930s. Its claims of formally equal treatment coexist with an explicit defense of severe controls intended to protect the national polity and suppress material considered potentially insulting to the emperor, making it useful for studying expanding ideological control before the Pacific War. The file also preserves the practical concerns of foreign residents and consular officials—delayed delivery, total confiscation rather than excision, and the absence of a clear public policy—while its cross-reference sheets reveal how related evidence was dispersed across the State Department’s decimal filing system.
